item.title: rtk-ai/rtk
item.description:
CLI proxy that reduces LLM token consumption by 60-90% on common dev commands. Single Rust binary, zero dependencies

https://www.rtk-ai.app

The cost reduction engine for AI coding agents.
Install it and forget it, then go as far as you want with pipelines.

Install • Pipelines • Docs • Website • RTK Pro • Discord

English • Francais • 中文 • 日本語 • 한국어 • Espanol • Português


① Install & forget: up to 90% less command output. Test runs, diffs, logs and builds are compressed before your agent reads them. 100+ commands, under 25 ms per command, no config, nothing changes in how you work. rtk gain shows what you saved.

② Go further with pipelines, as far as you take it. Hand heavy reads to a cheaper model, compress more than bash, clean the API traffic without breaking the prompt cache. One agent-agnostic file: start from a built-in, install one someone shared, or write and share your own. The community built the bash compressor 85k developers starred. Now it is building pipelines: the best one listed today cuts total cost by 20.2% in its author's benchmark.

Agents across the whole company? RTK Pro is the control layer for every AI agent: one gateway for every AI call, costs, secrets and personal data, policies, team catalog, audit. Discover RTK Pro ↓



Install & forget

macOS, and Linux with Homebrew

brew install rtk

Windows, with winget

winget install rtk-ai.rtk

Linux, macOS or WSL, with the install script

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh

Then plug it into your agent

rtk init -g                      # Claude Code; every other agent: see "Works in your agent"

Restart your agent. That's it: when it runs git status, RTK runs rtk git status and the agent reads a 3-line summary instead of 40 lines. Nothing to learn, nothing to call, and upgrading RTK never changes this.

Another project named "rtk" exists on crates.io. Check you have this one: rtk gain must show the savings dashboard, not "command not found".

Cargo, pre-built binaries, native Windows, WSL and uninstall: Installation guide · per-agent setup and --dry-run: Quick Start


Measure it: rtk gain

Every command RTK touches is counted on your machine. One command shows what it saved, today and since you installed it.

rtk gain                        # Summary stats
rtk gain --graph                # ASCII graph (last 30 days)
rtk gain --history              # Recent command history
rtk gain --daily                # Day-by-day breakdown
rtk gain --all --format json    # JSON export for dashboards

rtk discover                    # Find missed savings opportunities
rtk discover --all --since 7    # All projects, last 7 days

rtk session                     # Show RTK adoption across recent sessions

What the numbers mean. The compressor reduces the command output your agent reads, which is one part of the input tokens, which are one part of the bill: a 90% cut in command output is not a 90% cut in cost. Token counts are estimated as bytes / 4, so the percentages are reliable and the absolute numbers are approximate.

After a week of data, rtk gain ends with one line about RTK Pro, at most once a day and only on a terminal. pro_hint = false under [display] in config.toml turns it off.

Full explanation: How RTK Savings Work · attribution, the live dashboard and export formats: Token Savings Analytics


Out of the box: the bash compressor

The part 85k developers starred. Built by 200+ contributors, written against real command output, and every filter has to cut at least 20% to ship.

Operation What the agent reads
cargo test / npm test / pytest / go test Failures only, with their assertion; passing tests collapsed to a count
git status / git diff / git log Compact status, reduced diff context, one line per commit
git add/commit/push A confirmation line instead of progress output
ls / tree / grep / rg Trees with counts, matches grouped by file, long lines cut
ruff check / eslint / cargo clippy Grouped by rule and file
docker ps / kubectl Essential fields only

100+ commands across Git, GitHub CLI, Cargo/Rust, JavaScript (npm, pnpm, vitest, jest, tsc, Next.js, Angular, Playwright, Prisma), Python (ruff, pytest, mypy, pip), Go (go test, golangci-lint), Ruby, .NET, JVM (Gradle, Maven), PHP, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Terraform, and the file/search builtins. Every command and its filter: What RTK Optimizes

Three promises

  • Never blocks. If a filter fails, you get the raw output, and the command's exit code is passed through unchanged.
  • Never worse. RTK never prints more than the command did.
  • Nothing hidden. Output that is cut says where the full version is, and rtk bypass runs any command unfiltered, still tracked in rtk gain:
rtk bypass git log --oneline -20        # full git log, no truncation
rtk bypass npm install express          # raw npm output

The hook rewrites shell commands. Built-in tools such as Read, Grep and Glob pass through untouched out of the box; in Claude Code, a pipeline compresses them too (see Pipelines below).

Does RTK break the prompt cache? No: output is filtered once, before it enters the conversation. Details.


Want to go further? Pipelines.

Out of the box, RTK compresses command output and stops there. A pipeline is how you ask it for more: one small file that tells RTK what to do with what your agent reads and sends. No file means the compressor above and nothing else; a pipeline adds one thing at a time, and you can take it back out.

What people turn on first

  • Compress everything the agent reads, not just shell output: grep results, web pages, lockfiles, any output RTK has no filter for (Claude Code).
  • Hand big file reads to a cheaper model you choose. The file never enters your agent's context (Claude Code, with your API key).
  • Clean the API traffic your agent re-sends every turn, with the prompt cache kept intact (through the optional proxy, below).
  • Make the agent write less: terse prose, with code, paths, commands and errors kept in full (every agent).

Each of these is a built-in pipeline, one line to turn on. rtk-ai.app/pipelines lists them next to the pipelines the community shares, each with what it saved and how that was measured. Installing one is a single command:

rtk pipeline add github:user/repo        # check and install a shared pipeline

A pipeline can rewrite commands and send content to the models it declares, so read its file before you install it. Written once, a pipeline works in every agent RTK supports, as far as that agent's hooks allow: Agent Coverage shows what runs where.

Start here: Pipelines · the built-ins, explained: Reference Pipelines · write and share your own: Writing a Pipeline, Pipeline Commands

RTK Proxy (optional)

The rtk-proxy daemon runs the same pipeline on your agent's provider-API traffic: it strips bytes no model ever needed without breaking the prompt cache, and carries the calls your pipeline routes to cheaper models on the credential your agent already sends, so they show up in rtk gain. rtk init -g offers to set it up; rtk claude starts it and launches Claude through it with no configuration at all.

rtk claude              # start the daemon if needed, then launch Claude through it
rtk llm-proxy status    # is it up
rtk gain                # savings, command filtering and proxy side by side

Separate binary, separate licence (BUSL-1.1), its own rtk-proxy-<target> archive: rtk never links it. Not the same thing as rtk bypass, which runs one local command unfiltered.

Setup and subcommands: RTK Proxy · what it compresses: What the Proxy Compresses · settings and endpoints: Proxy Configuration



Agents across the whole company? Know what they cost, what they touch, and who ran what.

RTK runs on each developer's machine. RTK Pro connects them into one control layer for the whole company:

  • Gateway. Every AI call goes through one place, whichever provider each team uses.
  • Cost control. Spend by team, person and model. Waste found and removed. Budgets that warn, then stop.
  • Shield. Secrets and personal data masked before any model sees them.
  • Policies. Risky commands stopped before they run.
  • Team catalog. Skills, MCP servers and pipelines, assigned per team and project.
  • Audit log. Who did what, and whether it was allowed.

Agent2API is an AI routing gateway with Agent client takeover. It exposes a unified model API for custom AI providers and centralizes account routing, model mapping, gateway keys and request reports. It also manages local Agent clients' connection profiles, including importing, switching and previewing configuration changes.

✨ Key Features

  • 🔌 Unified model APIs — OpenAI Chat / Responses / Images and Anthropic Messages, with a unified model catalog; Raccoon, Loomy, Antigravity, ModelScope, WorkBuddy and Doubao Work supply image generation, while Raccoon, Loomy, Antigravity, ModelScope and WorkBuddy also support reference-image editing. Both are available as AI assistant tools
  • 🧭 AI routing — model mapping, account priority, load balancing, session affinity and failover in one place
  • 🤖 Agent client takeover — manage multiple connection profiles for local clients, import existing settings, preview writes and switch between the gateway and custom services
  • 🧩 Plugin extensions — additional provider implementations are installed and updated separately, not bundled with the application; custom providers do not require them
  • 🛡️ Egress proxies — select proxy-pool exits for accounts and update tasks
  • 🔑 Gateway security — scoped gateway keys, optional human verification for panel sign-in, and model requests refused by default until a key is configured
  • 📊 Request reports — request volume, success rate, token usage, cache hit rate and a 365-day heatmap
  • ⏰ Background maintenance — model catalog refresh, credential maintenance and software update checks; daily check-in runs per provider on that provider's own window (Qoder 10:01, ZCode 19:01, others follow the schedule time), plus a catch-up round that only touches accounts not yet checked in; additional provider-specific tasks are supplied by plugins
  • 🖥️ Three deployment forms — Windows / macOS / Linux desktop apps, headless Windows / Linux servers and Docker (amd64 / arm64); no Node runtime required, with a six-language interface

Three forms — pick the one that matches your setup; the complete install, upgrade, uninstall and troubleshooting guide is in Installation & deployment.

🔧 Development & Build

Requirements

  • Rust >= 1.77 and the Tauri 2 toolchain (to compile the desktop app itself; Windows also needs the WebView2 runtime)
  • Node.js >= 18.17 (only to run npm run tauri:* and frontend build scripts; the desktop app does not depend on Node at runtime)
  • Target platforms: Windows / macOS / Linux desktops, headless Windows / Linux servers, and a Docker server

Common scripts

npm run tauri:install      # Install desktop dependencies (same as npm --prefix desktop-tauri install)
npm run tauri:dev          # Launch the desktop app in dev mode (with hot reload)
npm run tauri:build        # Build the desktop installer

npm run build:icon         # Generate the icon source image (run after changing the icon design, then run tauri icon)

The build artifact is target/release/bundle/nsis/Agent2API_<version>_x64-setup.exe (about 8.6 MB as of 3.0; src-tauri/.cargo/config.toml points cargo's target-dir at the project root's target/).

The macOS .dmg can only be built on macOS (npm --prefix desktop-tauri run build -- --target universal-apple-darwin) — it cannot be cross-compiled from Windows, so the official artifact comes from the CI build workflow (macos-latest, two targets merged). Docker images and the server archives used for in-container updates come from the same workflow's linux-server job, which reuses the Dockerfile's compile path so the executable inside is built from the same toolchain as the image.
